name: echo-pair-wireless
description: Point to point with nothing on the wire: the message goes over the air and so does the ACK. Each node uses one radio full duplex — data on RF A, the acknowledgement on RF B at a different frequency — so the two machines need no network path between them at all. The wireless sibling of echo-pair-radio, which sends over the air but ACKs over TCP.

nodes.note: transmits the message on RF A and LISTENS for the ACK on RF B. Both blocks are on the same radio and must be: the modem's rf ACK requires one device driving both paths (tx-args == rx-args), which is why the subdevs differ and the frequencies do not collide.

mirror image: RECEIVES the message on RF A at 915 and ACKs on RF B at 925. The frequencies match the transmitter's by construction — each direction has its own carrier, which is what makes the link full duplex rather than half.

links.note: up carries the data at 915, down carries the stop-and-wait ACK at 925. Declaring the down medium wireless is what selects --ack-transport rf; it is refused unless the replying node declares a tx block, because a radio that cannot transmit cannot acknowledge.

note: BEFORE RUNNING: replace the two serials with your own from `uhd_find_devices`, and set each node's host to the machine its radio is attached to — 127.0.0.1 for both only when one machine holds both radios. TWO CARRIERS, not one: data at 915 and ACK at 925 here, and the separation has to be wide enough that each receiver does not hear its own transmitter. Run ./prepare.sh on BOTH radios, once per receive band, so the detector settings for each direction come from a survey rather than these defaults. If the data decodes but no ACK ever arrives, check the ACK direction first — it is a second link with its own antenna, gain and carrier, and it is the half that has no symptoms of its own until the transmitter starts retransmitting. ACK over TCP instead is echo-pair-radio.
